newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Kuchma blasts government, parliament.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Kuchma blasts government, parliament.

text.p: Ukraine President Leonid Kuchma, under pressure from foreign lenders, unpaid workers and hungry pensioners, told his government on Friday to shift a mountainous backlog of unpaid wages and payments or quit.

"If decisive steps are not taken to remove budget debts, the government should resign," Kuchma said in his most public and blistering attack in months against the cabinet led by Prime Minster Pavlo Lazarenko.
"We are in financial chaos," he added in a "state of the nation" address in parliament that lasted almost 90 minutes and was carried live on national television to the country's 51 million people.
As of March 1, according to central bank data, the government owed 4.2 billion hryvnias ($2.3 billion) to workers and 1.1 billion hryvnias to pensioners.
The non-payments crisis brought tens of thousands of protesters on to the streets for a "Day of Action" on March 18.

Viktor Suslov, a prominent deputy who heads parliament's finance commission, said Kuchma's demands meant the government might as well resign now since not even a "giant" could budge the non-payments mountain.
"The government has been set the impossible task of paying this debt or resigning. That means one thing. This was a proposal that it should resign," Suslov told reporters.

The government and parliament has also failed to pass a 1997 budget, slowing progress in talks with the International Monetary Fund on a multi-billion-dollar loan and leaving state coffers with no revenues.
"I would like to stress that the government bears responsibility for the absence of the budget," Kuchma said, adding that parliament was also guilty of slowing the process.
But Lazarenko, whose impending sacking has been widely rumoured in local media,drew the worst of the criticism.
"What was guiding the government and especially Lazarenko when they presented parliament with an absolutely unrealistic 1997 draft budget?" Kuchma asked.
Kuchma has sacked a string of ministers, dismissing four at once last month, including the economy and finance ministers.
He said these dismissals would only have the desired effect if big changes in the administration were made too.
A quarter of Ukraine's "chynovnyky" -- or civil servants in ministries and his administration -- would have to go, he said.
And Lazarenko's office should treat ministers with more respect. "We must raise the status of ministers who the cabinet of ministers' staff often see as little boys," he said.
Kuchma's speech avoided foreign affairs and relations with Russia which have been thorny since independence in 1991.
The neighbouring Slav states have never signed a post-Soviet friendship treaty which has been held up by disagreements over the fate of the Black Sea Fleet on Ukraine's Crimea peninsula.
Instead he focused on domestic affairs, saying Ukraine had embraced the path of reform and there was "no turning back".
He said the only way to interpret the failure to pass the budget was an attempt to force him to push it through by decree -- a step he would not take as it was unconstitutional.
"Dear people's deputies, the issue of dissolving parliament by decree could be put with just as much success," he said.
"Provoking me into taking unconstitutional action will not succeed," he added, to hoots from deputies who blame the government for not coming up with a revised document to debate.
